newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwanese shocked by S.Africa's China shift.
newsitem.headline: Taiwanese shocked by S.Africa's China shift.

text.p: Officials and ordinary people in Taiwan reacted with disbelief after President Nelson Mandela announced late on Wednesday that South Africa was dropping recognition of Taiwan in favour of Beijing.

State radio said a festive dinner party for high-ranking government officials turned sour when Foreign Minister John Chang got a telephone call some 30 minutes before Mandela's Johannesburg news conference.
"Minister Chang, without his usual smile, rushed out to answer a telephone call. He gravely reported something to Vice President and Premier Lien Chan and quickly left," it said.
Mandela told a news conference at his Johannesburg home that South Africa was recognising the communist People's Republic of China and at the same time downgrading relations with Taiwan.
He said it would be a gradual process he hoped could be completed within a year.
In and around the capital's nearly deserted late-night streets, reactions were mixed.
"Are you kidding? It's so sudden," a 22-year-old bartender surnamed Shen said with shock in his voice as he wiped a table at a popular Taipei pub.

South Africa was the biggest of Taiwan's 30 diplomatic allies, which include the Vatican and several underdeveloped states in Central America and Africa that benefit from wealthy Taiwan's generous foreign aid.
But some people said they were not surprised.
"We knew it was going to happen sooner or later. I'm more surprised that Taiwan-South Africa ties could last so long," said Tseng Chi-cheng, a Taipei engineer.
Property agent Chen Cheng-fu seemed resigned to the move.
"We should have expected this. From South Africa's point of view, if mainland China can offer them a better deal, why should they settle for less?" Chen said.
"It's all because Taiwan is not an independent country," said taxi driver Chen Cheng-hung, blaming the ruling Nationalist government's "One China" policy.
Beijing has seen Taiwan as a rebel province since the communists' 1949 civil war victory sent the defeated Nationalist government into exile on the island off the southeast coast.
Beijing has obliged all countries with which it establishes diplomatic ties to drop Taiwan, though it allows its friends to maintain economic and other unofficial ties with the island.
"Who wants to have diplomatic ties with a part of China, when they can have ties with China?" taxi driver Chen said sarcastically.
